REL-300.name: Listener, Timer or Subscription Registered in a Lifecycle Without Matching Cleanup
REL-300.question: Does this function register a listener, timer, observer or subscription as part of setting something up, without removing it when that thing is torn down?

javascript: useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener(...) or setInterval(...) or store.subscribe(...) }) with no cleanup function returned
componentDidMount, connectedCallback or a constructor that adds listeners or timers with no removal in componentWillUnmount, disconnectedCallback or a dispose method
tsx: a React effect or hook that subscribes, observes or starts a timer and returns no cleanup
python: an object's __init__ or setup connects a signal, registers a callback or starts a timer with no disconnect in close, __exit__ or teardown

javascript: the effect returns a function that removes the listener, clears the timer or unsubscribes
the listener uses { once: true } or an AbortSignal that is aborted on teardown
the registration is made once at module load for the program's lifetime
python: teardown disconnects or cancels the registration
the registration uses a weak reference or lives for the whole program

distinguish_from.CWE-401: memory is allocated and never freed, rather than a callback registration being left behind

REL-301.name: Wall-Clock Time Used to Measure Elapsed Time or Deadlines
REL-301.question: Does this function measure an elapsed time, timeout or deadline using wall-clock readings instead of a monotonic clock?

python: start = time.time() ... time.time() - start, or a deadline computed with datetime.now() and compared later
javascript: Date.now() - start or new Date() differences used for a timeout, retry delay, rate limit or benchmark
c: time(NULL), gettimeofday or clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) differences used as durations
cpp: std::chrono::system_clock::now() differences used for timeouts or measuring work
rust: SystemTime::now() with duration_since or elapsed used for a timeout or measurement

javascript: the wall-clock value is only stored or displayed

distinguish_from.REL-232: naive and time-zone-aware date-times are mixed

REL-302.name: Calendar Arithmetic With Fixed-Length Days, Months or Years
REL-302.question: Does this function advance or compare calendar dates by adding fixed numbers of seconds or days where days, months or years can differ in length?

any: 86400, 24 * 3600, 24*60*60*1000, 30 or 365 used to compute tomorrow, next month, next year or an age from local date-times
python: timedelta(days=30) for one month or timedelta(days=365) for one year, or adding 86400 to a local timestamp
javascript: date.getTime() + 24*60*60*1000 for the next local day, or setDate(getDate() + 30) for next month
c: adding 86400 to a time_t and then calling localtime to get the next calendar day
rust: Duration::from_secs(86400) added to a local date-time for the next day

any: the values are UTC instants and a fixed duration is truly meant
a calendar-aware API steps months and years
python: dateutil.relativedelta, date + timedelta(days=1) on a plain date, or zoneinfo-aware arithmetic is used
javascript: Temporal, date-fns addMonths or addDays, or Luxon is used
c: mktime normalises a struct tm whose tm_mday or tm_mon was incremented
rust: chrono Months, checked_add_months or NaiveDate succ is used

distinguish_from.REL-232: naive and aware date-times are mixed rather than stepped by fixed amounts

REL-303.name: Digit-String Identifier Parsed Into a Numeric Type
REL-303.question: Does this function convert a phone number, postcode, account number or other digit-string identifier into a numeric type?

python: int(phone), int(postcode), int(account_no) or float(card_number), then stored, compared or formatted
javascript: Number(zip), parseInt(phone) or +accountId on an identifier, or an ID longer than 15 digits handled as a number
c: atoi, atol or strtol on a phone number, postcode or account string that is then stored or compared
cpp: std::stoi or std::stoll on a phone number, postcode or account string
rust: phone.parse::<u64>() or postcode.parse::<u32>() and the number kept as the identifier
typescript: an identifier field declared as number in a type for data that arrives as digit strings

any: the identifier is kept as a string and validated with a pattern
the digits are parsed only to compute a checksum, with the string kept as the identifier
javascript: BigInt or a string is used for long identifiers

distinguish_from.REL-216: a parsed number is used without checking for NaN

REL-304.name: Human Name or Address Forced Into a Rigid Format
REL-304.question: Does this function validate, split or reformat a person's name or postal address using rules that only fit some cultures or countries?

any: a name checked against a pattern like ^[A-Za-z]+$ or [a-zA-Z ]{2,20} that rejects accents, apostrophes, hyphens or non-Latin scripts
a full name split on the first or last space into first and last name, or a surname made mandatory
an address required to have a house number, a state or a five-digit postcode regardless of country
the name is stored as entered with only length or control-character checks
address rules depend on the country and come from a maintained library
the field is not a person's name or a postal address

distinguish_from.CWE-20: input that should be restricted is not validated enough, rather than valid input being rejected

REL-305.name: Remote Call Retried in a Loop With No Attempt Limit or Backoff
REL-305.question: Does this function retry a failed network, database or service call in a loop with no attempt limit, or with no delay that grows between attempts?

any: while true or an unbounded loop that calls a remote service, catches the failure and loops again
a retry loop with a fixed short sleep or no sleep at all, and no maximum attempt count
javascript: a recursive retry function that calls itself on rejection with no attempt counter
python: while True: try: requests.get(...) break except RequestException: continue

any: attempts are capped and the delay grows, for example exponentially with jitter
a retry library or client retry policy such as tenacity, backoff, p-retry, tokio-retry or the SDK's built-in retries is used
the loop is a long-running consumer that waits on a blocking call rather than retrying a failure

distinguish_from.PERF-021: the loop polls a condition without sleeping rather than retrying a failed call
distinguish_from.CWE-1088: a call has no timeout, rather than unbounded retries

REL-306.name: Locale-Sensitive Case Conversion Used for Case-Insensitive Comparison
REL-306.question: Does this function compare text case-insensitively by converting case with a method that is locale-dependent or does not fold all Unicode characters?

python: a.lower() == b.lower() or upper() comparisons on user names, e-mail addresses or other text that can be non-ASCII
javascript: a.toLowerCase() === b.toLowerCase() or toLocaleUpperCase() on identifiers that may be compared across locales
c: tolower or toupper applied byte by byte to UTF-8 text before strcmp
strcasecmp on non-ASCII text under a user locale
cpp: std::tolower in a transform over a UTF-8 std::string before comparing
rust: to_lowercase() == on both sides for non-ASCII text that needs case folding

python: the strings are ASCII-only protocol tokens
javascript: localeCompare(b, undefined, { sensitivity: 'accent' or 'base' }) or Intl.Collator is used
c: the comparison is on ASCII-only tokens in the C locale
rust: eq_ignore_ascii_case on ASCII tokens, or a Unicode case-folding crate

distinguish_from.CWE-178: a security decision mishandles case differences, rather than an ordinary comparison
